passage:
There are about seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. Linguists estimate that half of them will fall silent before the end of this century. A language is considered to be in danger when children stop learning it, because once a generation is skipped the chain is almost impossible to repair.

Languages rarely vanish because speakers are forced to abandon them, although that has happened. More often the shift is gradual and voluntary. Parents notice that the national language brings better jobs and easier schooling, so they raise their children in it. Each family makes a sensible decision, and the sum of those decisions is the loss of a language.

What disappears with it is not only vocabulary. Many small languages carry detailed knowledge of the local environment — the names of hundreds of plants, the signs that predict weather, the routes that fish take through a river system. Botanists working in the Pacific have found species already named and described in local speech that were unknown to science.

Efforts to reverse the process have had mixed results. Recordings preserve a language but do not keep it alive. What works better is giving people reasons to use it every day: schools that teach in it, radio programmes, apps, road signs. Hebrew, revived after centuries with almost no native speakers, remains the outstanding success.

Most endangered languages will not follow that path. Many communities have decided, however, that recording their language carefully is worth doing even if fluency cannot be restored. Something written down can be studied; something forgotten cannot.
